episode_title: Where Is Alice? The Hidden Epidemic of Loneliness and the Power of Human Connection

real_qa.q: What inspired Patrick Durillo to create the alto.cool app?
real_qa.r: Patrick met Alice, an 84-year-old neighbor in Zurich, who shared that she had lost her husband and son and was feeling lonely. This personal encounter led him to research loneliness globally, discovering it was an epidemic affecting millions of people worldwide. He decided to take action and created alto.cool, an app that matches seniors and younger generations together to do social activities like playing cards and chess.

real_qa.q: What is the U-curve pattern of loneliness across age demographics?
real_qa.r: According to the BBC loneliness experiment by Professor Pamela Colter and professors Oakley and Kachopo from the University of Chicago, loneliness follows a U-curve pattern. Young people aged 17-29 experience high loneliness rates, then loneliness decreases during ages 30-40 when people are active with work and family, and increases again when people retire. However, the data showing people admitting loneliness is likely only the tip of the iceberg.
real_qa.requete: U-curve loneliness BBC Pamela Colter age demographics

real_qa.q: Is intergenerational connection common in Switzerland, and how can it be encouraged?
real_qa.r: Patrick states it is not common in Switzerland for younger people to reach out to older generations, as Swiss culture is known for being reserved and discreet. However, he believes reaching out is simpler than people think—it doesn't require grand gestures, just small steps like knocking on a neighbor's door, asking someone for coffee, sending a text, or making a call. Cross-generational mentoring programs he has run professionally have consistently been successful, with participants from different ages always reporting they learned much from each other.

real_qa.q: How does loneliness relate to business leadership and corporate culture?
real_qa.r: Patrick connects loneliness to leadership through his work with large American corporations over 20 years, noting that he became increasingly interested in how generations of leaders can pass knowledge to one another and how different generations perceive each other. He emphasizes that just because a leader is busy, active in business, or meets many people does not mean they are not feeling lonely. Building a healthy organizational culture involves recognizing and addressing the loneliness epidemic within teams and workplaces.
real_qa.requete: loneliness business leadership corporate culture intergenerational

real_qa.q: What is the main misconception about loneliness, and why is it underreported?
real_qa.r: A major misconception is that loneliness is only a problem affecting elderly people, when in fact it can touch anyone at any age—young, middle-aged, or old—at any point in time. Additionally, loneliness remains a taboo topic in Switzerland, the United States, and Europe generally. At a personal level, it is very rare to hear someone openly say 'I am lonely' or 'I feel lonely from time to time,' so the people admitting loneliness in surveys likely represent only the tip of the iceberg of actual prevalence.

He has conducted coaching and mentoring programs globally for large American corporations, with a focus on intergenerational leadership and knowledge transfer. His personal encounter with an 84-year-old lonely neighbor named Alice in February 2015 inspired him to research loneliness as a global epidemic and subsequently create alto.cool, an app matching seniors and younger generations for social activities.
